explanations.explanation: That's the assignment, friend. Paul says, "But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine." He doesn't say speak what's trendy or what gets a cheer. He says speak what matches the teaching, and Titus doesn't need a committee meeting to do that.

explanations.answer: Things the crowds want to hear
explanations.explanation: I get the temptation, friend. A crowd that loves you feels GOOD. But Paul never mentions what the crowds want here. He says to speak "the things that are consistent with sound doctrine." Chasing applause is a tiring way to spend a day.

explanations.answer: Things the town elders voted on
explanations.explanation: Nobody's passing around a ballot box in this verse, friend. Paul doesn't mention a vote at all. What he tells Titus to speak is "the things that are consistent with sound doctrine." That's the standard, and it's the teaching itself.

Right on target, friend. Paul says the older women are to be teachers of good, "In this way they can train the young women." So the older women have something to hand down, and the younger women are the ones receiving it. It's one generation passing the recipe to the next.
Paul never brings up money in this verse, friend. He says the older women can train "the young women." It's about age here, with older women teaching younger ones. Bank accounts don't come into it.
Good guess at a word, friend, but Paul doesn't say foreign. The verse says the older women can "train the young women." The line he draws is between older and younger. Passports aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: So the word of God won't be discredited
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Paul gives, friend. He says all this is "so that the word of God will not be discredited." The way they live is tied to how the word of God is seen. Paul doesn't make it complicated, and he doesn't need to.

explanations.answer: So the church in Crete will grow larger
explanations.explanation: Bigger would sound nice, friend, but Paul never says that here. His reason is "so that the word of God will not be discredited." He names the word of God, not the headcount. I'd rather stick with what the verse actually gives us.

explanations.answer: So their households will be admired in town
explanations.explanation: A house everybody admires sounds lovely, friend. But Paul doesn't give that as the reason. He says it's "so that the word of God will not be discredited." The point of the verse is the word of God, not the neighbors' opinion of the house.

Yes, friend, count it up. For the older men, Paul lists a whole run of things: temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. For the younger men, it's one line: "urge the younger men to be self-controlled." Short and to the point, like a text from a busy dad.

Take another look, friend. For the older men, Paul gives a long list in verse 2: temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. For the younger men, verse 6 says only, "urge the younger men to be self-controlled." So the word to the younger men is the shorter one by a mile.

Yes, friend. Paul says, "show yourself to be an example by doing good works." Titus isn't just supposed to tell people what to do, he's supposed to be what he's telling them. People watch the leader more than they listen to him. I know a stamper who learned that watching Mother Miller press dough.

That's a big job description, friend, and Paul doesn't give it here. What he says is to "show yourself to be an example by doing good works." Titus leads by living it. The robe and the gavel aren't in this verse.

Carrying messages is honest work, friend, but that's not what Paul asks here. He tells Titus to "show yourself to be an example by doing good works." The focus is on how Titus lives in front of the believers. His life is meant to be the lesson.

Careful with this one, friend. Paul says, "In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works." That's EVERYTHING, not just the big stuff. Nobody gets to be a hero on Sunday and a mystery the rest of the week.

That's right, friend. Paul writes, "In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works." He doesn't cut it down to only the big moments. The small moments count too, and it's the small ones nobody's clapping for.

explanations.answer: Leave them ashamed with nothing bad to say
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says, friend. He wants Titus's teaching above reproach "so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us." If the critic looks for something to pounce on and comes up empty, that's a quiet kind of win. I'd pay money to see that face.

explanations.answer: Win them over to the faith right away
explanations.explanation: That would be a happy ending, friend, but Paul doesn't promise it here. He says the opposer will be "ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us." No "right away," and no mention of winning them over. We keep to what the verse says.

explanations.answer: Drive them off the island of Crete
explanations.explanation: Whoa, friend, nobody's getting escorted to a boat. Paul says the one who opposes will be "ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us." Leaving Crete isn't in the verse. The whole idea is that the critic has nothing to use.

Paul closes that door, friend. He says slaves are to be "not stealing from them, but showing all good faith." No loophole for taking a little, and no "a small amount is fine." Not even a crumb-sized exception.

That's right, friend. Paul says "not stealing from them, but showing all good faith." There's no allowance for taking a little here and there. It's a clear line, and it comes with all good faith instead.

explanations.answer: Make it beautiful in every way
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says "in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior." Adorn is a decorating word, so the way they live makes the teaching look lovely to everyone watching. And he says in EVERY respect, so none of it is left plain.

Simple is nice, friend, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says "in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior." To adorn is to make something look good, not to make it easier. The teaching doesn't change, and how it looks does.

I wish everything came with a built-in memory trick, friend. But Paul says "in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior." Adorning is about how it looks, not how well it sticks. So the answer is about beauty, not memory.

That's the pair, friend. Paul says grace "instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions." So grace isn't only a gift we receive, it's a teacher that points us in a direction. And he follows it right away with how to live.

My ovens would be sad if that were the answer, friend. Paul says grace teaches us to renounce "ungodliness and worldly passions." Hard work and planning aren't on that list. What he follows with is living sensible, upright, and godly lives.

No, friend, Paul isn't telling anyone to leave their people behind. He says grace "instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions." Those are the things to renounce. Friends and family aren't named in that verse at all.

Hold on, friend, Paul says the opposite. Grace instructs us "to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age." Present age means now, not someday. There's no waiting room before the godly living starts.

Right, friend. Paul says grace teaches us "to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age." That's now, with no delay built in. Nobody has to wait until they're older, wiser, or have more free time.

That's the One, friend. Paul says we await "the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." Our hope has a name, and the name is Jesus. Everything else in the passage leans toward that.

Elijah, a prophet of Israel, is a great name, friend, but he's not the one Paul has in mind. The verse says we await "the glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." Paul names Jesus Christ, plain as day.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a giant of the faith, friend, but he's not who Paul points to here. Paul says we await "the glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." The hope is Jesus, and Paul says so outright.
That's the word, friend. Paul says Jesus "gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness." Notice the word ALL. He gave Himself for us, and that's a gift big enough to carry the whole thing.

I can see why that came to mind, friend, but Paul doesn't say poverty here. He says Jesus "gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness." That's the word the verse uses, and it covers a lot of ground.

That's an understandable pick, friend, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul says Jesus "gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness." So that's what this verse says He redeems us from. We stay with Paul's words.

Yes, friend. Paul says Jesus purifies "a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds." Zealous means eager, so these folks aren't dragging their feet. They're the ones first in line to help with the dishes.

A big title looks great on a business card, friend, but Paul doesn't mention one here. He says this people is "zealous for good deeds." The eagerness is for doing good, not for what's printed under your name.

Some folks do love a long debate, friend, and I've heard a few. But Paul says this people is "zealous for good deeds." The eagerness he names is for doing, not arguing. Debates don't show up in the verse.
Yes, friend, it's both. Paul says to speak these things "as you encourage and rebuke with all authority." Rebuke sits right next to encourage in the same sentence. Titus gets the two jobs together.
Look again, friend. The verse says, "Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority." So rebuke is right there, side by side with encourage. Paul asks Titus to do both.
That's the word, friend. Paul ends with "Let no one despise you." Titus is to speak with all authority, and Paul doesn't want anyone looking down on him. Strong ending to a strong letter.

Envy would be a different problem, friend, and Paul doesn't bring it up. The verse says, "Let no one despise you." The word is despise, which is about being looked down on. That's the one Titus has to watch for.

Flattery sounds pleasant, friend, so I see the pull. But Paul says, "Let no one despise you." He's talking about being looked down on, not about being buttered up. That's the line he leaves Titus with.
